# Basic Concepts {.hero #s03-probability}

::: {.sem-mark data-sem="3"}
Seminar 3 · Conditional probability and Bayes
:::

## Probability of an Event {.formula-slide #prob-count}

::: {.lede-min}
Count how many ways the event can happen, then how many things can happen at all. The probability is the ratio of the two.
:::

$$P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \frac{\#\ \text{ways } \color{#93C54B}{A} \text{ can happen}}{\#\ \text{of things that can happen}} = \frac{|\color{#93C54B}{A}|}{|\Omega|}$$

:::: {.two-col}
::: {}
[Flip a coin twice]{.col-head}

$\Omega = \{hh,\ ht,\ th,\ tt\} \quad \color{#6E7681}{\text{4 in all}}$

```{=html}
<div class="coin-row">
<svg width="246" height="34" viewBox="0 0 246 34" aria-label="the four outcomes of two coin flips">
<g font-family="Roboto, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle">
<circle cx="13" cy="17" r="11" fill="rgba(147,197,75,0.18)" stroke="#93C54B" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="13" y="22" fill="#5E8A1E">H</text>
<circle cx="39" cy="17" r="11" fill="rgba(147,197,75,0.18)" stroke="#93C54B" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="39" y="22" fill="#5E8A1E">H</text>
<circle cx="75" cy="17" r="11" fill="rgba(147,197,75,0.18)" stroke="#93C54B" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="75" y="22" fill="#5E8A1E">H</text>
<circle cx="101" cy="17" r="11" fill="none" stroke="#B0B7C0" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="101" y="22" fill="#6E7681">T</text>
<circle cx="137" cy="17" r="11" fill="none" stroke="#B0B7C0" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="137" y="22" fill="#6E7681">T</text>
<circle cx="163" cy="17" r="11" fill="rgba(147,197,75,0.18)" stroke="#93C54B" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="163" y="22" fill="#5E8A1E">H</text>
<circle cx="199" cy="17" r="11" fill="none" stroke="#B0B7C0" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="199" y="22" fill="#6E7681">T</text>
<circle cx="225" cy="17" r="11" fill="none" stroke="#B0B7C0" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="225" y="22" fill="#6E7681">T</text>
</g>
</svg>
</div>
```

[At least one head]{.col-lab}

$\color{#93C54B}{A} = \{hh,\ ht,\ th\} \qquad P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \tfrac{3}{4} = 75\%$

[No heads]{.col-lab}

$\color{#325D88}{B} = \{tt\} \qquad P(\color{#325D88}{B}) = \tfrac{1}{4} = 25\%$
:::

::: {}
[Roll two dice]{.col-head}

::: {.dice-grid}
<div id="dicegrid-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

$\Omega = \{11,\ 12,\ \ldots,\ 66\} \quad \color{#6E7681}{\text{36 in all}}$

[At least one five]{.col-lab}

$\color{#93C54B}{A} = \{15, 25, 35, 45, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 65\}$

$P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \tfrac{11}{36}$

[Or split on the first die]{.col-lab}

$P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \tfrac{1}{6} + \tfrac{5}{6} \times \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{6}{36} + \tfrac{5}{36} = \tfrac{11}{36}$
:::
::::

::: {.pitfall}
A tempting answer is 6 + 6 = 12, six rolls with a five on the first die and six with a five on the second. Five and five is in both lists, so twelve counts it twice. The split on the right avoids that, because its second case needs the first die not to be a five.
:::

## Sample Spaces and Events {.stage-slide #space-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Roll two dice and every possible result is on the board. The sample space $\Omega$ is that whole board, and an **event** is any part of it you can point at.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="space-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="space-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="space-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="space-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
When every outcome is equally likely, a probability is a count. $P(\color{#93C54B}{A})$ is the cells in $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ over the cells in $\Omega$. Two fair dice earn that assumption, and most real problems do not.
:::

## Unions, Intersections and Complements {.stage-slide #setops-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Two events on the same board. $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}$ is "either", $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}$ is "both", and $\color{#93C54B}{A}^{c}$ is everything left over.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="setops-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="setops-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="setops-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="setops-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
Add 6 and 18 and you get 24, which is three too many. The cells that belong to both events were counted twice, so they have to come back off.
:::

## The Same Picture, Drawn as Circles {.stage-slide #venn-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
A **Venn diagram** is the board with the grid rubbed out. The four counts are the ones you just read off it, and they still add to 36.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="venn-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="venn-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="venn-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="venn-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
These circles are drawn to scale, so $\color{#325D88}{B}$ really does cover three times the area of $\color{#93C54B}{A}$. Most are not, which is why the counts written on them matter more than the picture.
:::

## Set Notation for Probability {.formula-slide #set-formal}

::: {.lede-min}
Counting gives $P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = |\color{#93C54B}{A}|/|\Omega|$ and $P(\color{#93C54B}{A}^{c}) = 1 - P(\color{#93C54B}{A})$. Two rules do the rest.
:::

:::: {.fragment}
::: {.rule-label .rule-or}
[Either]{.rw} · $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}$
:::

$$\begin{array}{@{}l@{\;\;}c@{\;\;}l@{}}
P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}) & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) + P(\color{#325D88}{B}) - P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})\\[4pt]
\phantom{P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})} & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) + P(\color{#325D88}{B}) \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{if mutually exclusive}}
\end{array}$$
::::

:::: {.fragment}
::: {.rule-label .rule-and}
[Both]{.rw} · $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}$
:::

$$\begin{array}{@{}l@{\;\;}c@{\;\;}l@{}}
P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}) & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) \times P(\color{#325D88}{B} \mid \color{#93C54B}{A})\\[4pt]
\phantom{P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})} & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) \times P(\color{#325D88}{B}) \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{if independent}}
\end{array}$$
::::

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
Mutually exclusive means $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B} = \varnothing$, so there is nothing to subtract. Independent means learning $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ tells you nothing about $\color{#325D88}{B}$, which the next slide makes precise.
:::

## Conditional Probabilities {.formula-slide #conditional-probabilities}

::: {.lede-min}
Being told that $\color{#325D88}{B}$ happened throws away every outcome outside it. What is left is a smaller sample space, and the question is how much of that is $\color{#93C54B}{A}$.
:::

::: {.cond-row}

$$P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{B}) = \frac{P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})}{P(\color{#325D88}{B})}$$
:::

Six rolls survive and one of them starts with a three, so $P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{B}) = \tfrac{1}{6}$, which is $P(\color{#93C54B}{A})$ over again. The dice are **independent**.

::::

::: {.note-box}
Here $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ is "the first die is a three". Reversing the bar asks something else, and that is what Bayes is for.
:::


## Conditioning Narrows the Sample Space {.stage-slide #cond-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Eight in ten office managers would buy the software ($\color{#93C54B}{A}$), and four in ten of those would also upgrade ($\color{#325D88}{B}$). Of the rest, one in ten would. Given $\color{#325D88}{B}$, how likely is $\color{#93C54B}{A}$?
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="cond-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cond-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cond-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cond-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
Learning $\color{#325D88}{B}$ throws the other 66% away, so $P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{B}) = P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})/P(\color{#325D88}{B})$.
:::

## The Law of Total Probability {.formula-slide #total-probability}

::: {.lede-min}
Cut $\Omega$ into pieces that do not overlap and leave nothing out. Every outcome in $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ then lies in exactly one piece, so the probability of $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ is its slices added back up.
:::

::: {.cond-row}

$$P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \sum_{i} P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{B_i})\, P(\color{#325D88}{B_i})$$
:::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {}
[Supplier 1]{.col-head}
[Half the parts, two per hundred faulty]{.col-sub}

$$0.50 \times 0.02 = 0.010$$
:::

::: {}
[Supplier 2]{.col-head}
[Three parts in ten, four per hundred faulty]{.col-sub}

$$0.30 \times 0.04 = 0.012$$
:::

::: {}
[Supplier 3]{.col-head}
[One part in five, seven per hundred faulty]{.col-sub}

$$0.20 \times 0.07 = 0.014$$
:::
::::

::: {.note-box}
Adding the three routes gives $P(\text{faulty}) = 0.036$. Ask instead which supplier sent the faulty part in your hand, and you are asking for Bayes.
:::


## Librarian or Farmer? {.stage-slide #bayes-hook}

::: {.lede-min}
Steve is very shy and withdrawn, invariably helpful but with very little interest in people or in the world of reality. A meek and tidy soul, he has a need for order and structure, and a passion for detail.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-prior}
<div id="prior-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="prior-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="prior-frag-2"}

::: {.slide-footer}
The description never changes; the answer does — because of a number that is not in it. That number is the base rate, and the next slide goes and counts it.
:::

## Twenty Farmers for Every Librarian {.stage-slide #bayes-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-bayes}
<div id="bayes-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-3"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-4"}

::: {.slide-footer}
The base rate is how common each job is, before you read a word about Steve. His description fits librarians four times better. But there are twenty times more farmers, so he is still five times more likely to be one.
:::

## Move the Prior, Watch the Answer Move {.sim-slide #bayes-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 3 · the base rate does the work
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
prior <- 1 / 21 # <-- P(librarian)
n <- 300000

lib  <- runif(n) < prior

# fits 40% of librarians, 10% of farmers
fits <- runif(n) < ifelse(lib, 0.40, 0.10)

c("P(H)" = prior, "P(H|E)" = mean(lib[fits]))
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
The evidence is identical every time — only the prior changes. `1/21` is the real ratio, one librarian for every twenty farmers; at `0.50` you get 0.80. **The description never had an opinion about how common librarians are, so the base rate has to supply it.**
:::

## Combinatorics and the Factorial {.formula-slide #combinatorics}

::: {.lede-min}
There are $n$ choices and you are taking $r$ of them. Two questions settle which formula you need, whether you sample with replacement and whether the order matters.
:::

$$n! = n \times (n-1) \times \cdots \times 2 \times 1 \qquad 0! = 1$$

::::: {.three-col}
::: {}
[With replacement]{.col-head}
[Order matters]{.col-sub}

$$n^{\,r}$$

[Ten coin flips in a row]{.col-lab}

$2^{10} = 1{,}024$
:::

::: {}
[Without replacement]{.col-head}
[Order matters]{.col-sub}
[Permutation · $^{n}P_{r}$]{.col-term}

$$\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$$

[Five cards off the top of the deck]{.col-lab}

$\begin{array}{@{}r@{\;}c@{\;}l@{}}
\dfrac{52!}{47!} & = & 52 \times 51 \times 50 \times 49 \times 48 \\[3pt]
 & = & 311{,}875{,}200
\end{array}$
:::

::: {}
[Without replacement]{.col-head}
[Order does not matter]{.col-sub}
[Combination · $^{n}C_{r}$]{.col-term}

$$\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!} = \dbinom{n}{r}$$

[One hand, dealt either way]{.col-lab}

::: {.stack}
```{=html}
<div class="perm-row"><span>K Q 2 3 7</span><span>K 2 Q 7 3</span></div>
```

$\dbinom{52}{5} = 2{,}598{,}960$
:::
:::
:::::

::: {.note-box}
The last two differ by $r!$, the orders the $r$ you picked could have come in. Those 311,875,200 runs collapse to 2,598,960 hands because one hand can be dealt $5! = 120$ ways.
:::
